title: Ratna Manikya Mints the Ruby Coins

title_i18n.en: Ratna Manikya Mints the Ruby Coins

subtitle: A hostage prince turns borrowed mint and script into the mark of Manikya rule
region: Tripura court, Bengal Sultanate frontier and Ujjayanta coin collections
moral: Borrowed tools can become signs of independent power.

sources.citation: Coins of Ratna Manikya I, c. 1467 onward, Ujjayanta Palace museum corpus
sources.note: Primary evidence for the corrected chronology and first secure Manikya coinage.

sources.citation: Rajmala, canto on Ratna Manikya I
sources.note: Narrates the hostage episode, Bengali settlers and court reforms.

sources.citation: N.N. Bhattacharyya, Coinage of the Tripura Rajas (1986); Ramani Mohan Sarma (1987)
sources.note: Modern numismatic correction of the Rajmala sequence.

panels.shot: low-angle dramatic close-up on a single silver coin held between fingers, palace and forest hills blurred behind

dialogue.text: From hostage in a sultan’s court to king of the hills, Ratna Manikya I forged Tripura’s fate on small round coins of borrowed silver.

panels.shot: medium shot inside a Bengal Sultanate hall, with young Ratna in the background among courtiers

dialogue.text: The Rajmala remembers a Tripura prince sent to the Bengal Sultan, a hostage and a guest, watching another court’s power with sharp, quiet eyes.

panels.shot: over-the-shoulder shot of Ratna watching scribes and treasurers at work

dialogue.text: Here he saw registers in Persian hands, Kayastha scribes bending over ledgers, and silver disks weighed and counted with cold exact care.

panels.shot: tight close-up on Ratna’s face half in shadow, eyes reflecting the glint of coins and the map of Tripura

dialogue.speaker: ratna_manikya_i
dialogue.text: If their silver can bind a delta, what will it do in my hills?

panels.shot: wide shot of a forested frontier road as Ratna returns with a small, armed escort

dialogue.text: With support won in the delta plains, the prince rode back toward Tripura, the Rajmala says, no longer a mere son but a claimant, carrying new allies and old grudges.

panels.shot: sweeping wide shot of the Tripura hill stronghold as Ratna’s forces approach its gates

dialogue.text: The chroniclers do not soften what followed. Ratna seized the fort, drove his father into exile, and bound his brothers in prison to clear the path to the throne.

panels.shot: medium shot in a dim prison corridor, Ratna framed between barred doors, back to the viewer

dialogue.text: The same Rajmala that praises him as builder names him usurper. In its verses, power in Tripura changes hands not with smooth ritual, but with chains and exile.

panels.shot: ceremonial low-angle shot of Ratna on a wooden throne, priests and nobles around

dialogue.text: Yet from this hard beginning, a long reign took shape. Under Ratna Manikya I, the hill kingdom faced the Bengal Sultanate not as a mere fief, but as a wary neighbour.

panels.shot: bird’s-eye view of a caravan of families with ox-carts entering the Tripura hills

dialogue.text: Between about 1464 and 1468, the Rajmala speaks of some four thousand Bengali Hindu families brought into Tripura, their carts creaking with tools, icons and scripts.

panels.shot: medium interior shot of a new administrative hall with Bengali scribes at work

dialogue.text: Ratna set these settlers to work. Kayastha ministers rose in his court, bringing Bengali and Persian administrative practice into the hill kingdom’s daily grain and levy.

panels.shot: close-up on Ratna and a Kayastha minister over a map and tally sticks

dialogue.speaker: ratna_manikya_i
dialogue.text: Write their dues, and mine, so none can pretend forgetfulness.

panels.shot: evocative side view of an early mint workshop in action

dialogue.text: Then came the mint. Modern scholars date his coinage from about 1467, silver and copper disks in Bengal Sultanate fabric and weight, but now bearing Tripura’s own marks.

panels.shot: macro close-up on the face of a Ratna Manikya coin resting on a wooden table

dialogue.text: His coins spoke in Hindu legends—invoking Vishnu, Shiva, and the Chaturdasha Devata—even as they kept the delta’s tested weights and crisp, circular form.

panels.shot: medium shot of Ratna with priests and artisans discussing coin designs

dialogue.text: In this small space, he bound hill cults and court craft. The names of deities from Tripura’s shrines travelled outward, struck on metal that changed many hands.

panels.shot: low-angle shot of Ratna holding a coin before a shrine of the Chaturdasha Devata

dialogue.speaker: ratna_manikya_i
dialogue.text: Let the hills know this metal bears their guardians’ names.

panels.shot: medium shot of a merchant weighing Ratna’s coin against a Bengal Sultanate coin in a market

dialogue.text: In weight and feel, his silver matched the delta’s, easing trade. But where the Sultan’s coins bore Islamic invocations, Ratna’s bore Manikya titles and Tripura’s gods.

panels.shot: close-up on an older Ratna reading or handling one of his own coins thoughtfully

dialogue.text: Modern numismatists studying these pieces corrected even the Rajmala’s sequence, finding in their dates and styles a clearer calendar of his long, complex rule.

panels.shot: museum-style wide shot of a display case at Ujjayanta Palace with Ratna’s coins

dialogue.text: Today, in Ujjayanta’s cases, his coins survive where many chronicles fall silent, tiny silver witnesses that the Manikya title predated him, yet shone sharper under his hand.

panels.shot: final contemplative wide shot of a Tripura landscape as coins pass hand to hand in the foreground

dialogue.text: A prince who rose through exile, harsh in seizure and deft in statecraft, Ratna Manikya I turned borrowed mints and scripts into Tripura’s own voice in metal—a reminder that power often speaks through the smallest things.
